meta.tagline: The most Spanish city in Spain — and the one that earned it

pills: Eat tapas standing at the bar

overview.title: Welcome to Seville
overview.intro: Seville is the city that invented late nights and hosts the Holy Week procession that stops the entire country for a week. In July, the hottest city in Europe. In April, during Semana Santa and Feria de Abril, it transforms into something that has to be witnessed to be understood. The Alcázar is one of the most beautiful palaces ever built. The Cathedral is the largest Gothic structure in the world. But that is not the point. The point is the bar on Calle Gerona — where the bill is chalked on the wood and the same dish has been served since the Moors.

local_word.definition: In Seville, the tapas culture is specific: a small plate of food, ordered at the bar, eaten standing or perched on a high stool, accompanied by a caña (small beer) or a glass of fino sherry. The ritual is to move between bars — one drink and one tapa per bar, then on to the next. One drink, one plate, three or four bars, two streets, two hours. A Tuesday evening in Seville looks like this. No table, no reservation — just the bar counter and an evening passing by.

rules.title: Book the Alcázar and the Cathedral weeks ahead
rules.description: The Alcázar and Cathedral both run timed-entry systems that fill weeks ahead in April and May. No walk-ins. Book online before you arrive — the Alcázar especially. Its Mudejar interior makes a strong case for most beautiful palace in Spain that isn't the Alhambra.

rules.title: Lunch at 14:00, dinner at 21:00 — the city means it
rules.description: Kitchens open at 14:00. They close at 16:00. Not as a suggestion. Dinner starts at 21:00 — that's the opening time, not the peak. The table next to you at 22:30 will have three generations on it, including a child who should be asleep. Between 17:00 and 20:30: slow walk, café stop, glass of manzanilla on a terrace. That's the hinge of the day.

rules.title: In summer, the city moves at night
rules.description: July and August: regularly 42°C. The city doesn't fight it — it rearranges around it. Empty streets at 3pm. Full streets at 11pm. Out by 9am, inside by 13:00, back out at 19:00, stay out until the city forces you home. Arrive expecting summer logic from home and Seville will be miserable. Follow the local pattern and it's extraordinary.

quick_facts.label: Airport
quick_facts.sub: EA bus → Torre del Oro, ~35 min

quick_facts.label: Transport
quick_facts.sub: Single ticket €1.40 · 1-day pass €5 · 3-day pass €10 · contactless accepted

quick_facts.label: Weather
quick_facts.value: Hottest city in Europe in July
quick_facts.sub: Apr–Jun ideal · Jul–Aug brutal · Sep–Oct perfect · Dec–Feb mild

quick_facts.label: Tapa rule
quick_facts.sub: Order at the bar · caña + tapa · move between bars

tip.label: Monday free entry — plan around it
tip.text: Several of Seville's best monuments go free on Monday afternoons. Real Alcázar: free from 16:00 — book free tickets online well in advance, limited capacity. Casa de Pilatos: free 15:00–19:00, no booking, queue at the door. Palacio de las Dueñas: free from 16:00, book online same day. Torre del Oro: free all day Monday, no reservation. Four monuments. One Monday. Zero euros.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: Seville's historic centre is compact and flat. Most things are walkable. The bike network is the best in Spain. Use it.

items.title: Airport → City Centre
items.description: EA airport bus to Torre del Oro (riverside): every 30 minutes, 35 minutes, pay onboard. No train link. Taxis are metered. That's it.

items.title: MetroCentro tram — through the historic heart
items.description: MetroCentro tram runs Plaza Nueva → Cathedral → Archivo de Indias → Nervión. €1.40 — machines at stops or tap contactless on the validator. Tarjeta Turista: 1-day or 3-day unlimited tram and bus. Runs until midnight weekdays, 2am Fri–Sat.

items.title: Buses — the city backbone
items.description: 44 TUSSAM routes, red-and-yellow, cover everywhere the tram doesn't. €1.40, contactless works. C5 loops the historic centre. Night buses run until 5:30am at weekends — relevant when dinner starts at 21:30.

items.title: SEVIci bikes — the best way around
items.description: 180km+ of separated cycle lanes. Completely flat. SEVIci bikes: stations every few hundred metres, 7-day subscription for unlimited 30-minute trips. Alcázar to Triana bridge along the river — under 20 minutes. For anything under 3km: the bike is faster than anything else.

items.title: On foot — the only real option in the centre
items.description: Cathedral to Casa de Pilatos: 10 minutes. Triana bridge to Alcázar: 15 minutes. Alameda de Hércules to Plaza de España: 20 minutes. The patios, the orange trees, the Mudéjar tilework on ordinary corners — all between the monuments, not at them. Slow down.

callout.label: Guadalquivir river path — cycling at golden hour
callout.text: The Guadalquivir path south from Torre del Oro: city skyline on the left, river and herons on the right. An hour before sunset the stone turns a colour between copper and gold — specific to this latitude, this river, this hour. SEVIci bike: Torre del Oro to Triana bridge in 20 minutes. On foot: an hour. Both correct. Free at all hours.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: Every barrio is walkable from every other. Neighbourhood choice is about which city you wake up inside — Santa Cruz and Triana are not the same city.

local_word.definition: Each barrio has its own character and the locals mean it precisely. A person from Triana is not from Seville — they'll tell you so. Santa Cruz is the Seville tourists know. La Macarena is the one locals defend. El Arenal is where the Americas money was counted. Know which barrio you're in.

items.name: Santa Cruz
items.description: Streets too narrow for cars, too white for shade. Cathedral at the end of every other alley. Beautiful — and by 10am, belonging to everyone else. Stay here for monument proximity. Find another barrio for evenings.

items.name: El Arenal
items.description: The neighbourhood where the Americas gold arrived and was taxed. Plaza de Toros at one end, Guadalquivir at the other. Central but less theatrical than Santa Cruz. Best river access.

items.name: Triana
items.description: Triana is not Seville — culturally convinced it's something better, and not wrong. Azulejo tiles still fired by hand. Iron-and-glass market by the bridge. Bars on Calle Betis facing the Cathedral across the water. 15 minutes from centre. Feels like a different city.

items.name: La Macarena
items.description: Where Holy Week begins and is taken most seriously. Basílica de la Macarena — weeping Virgin, gold mantle, genuine devotion. Alameda de Hércules (1574): oldest public promenade in Europe, now lined with bars. No tourist trail. That's the point.

items.name: Centro / Alfalfa
items.description: Plaza del Salvador, Calle Sierpes — where Sevillanos actually shop and eat. Less picturesque than Santa Cruz, far more alive. The best tapas bars are scattered through here.

best_time.title: Best Time to Visit
best_time.intro: Seville has one genuinely difficult season. Every other month has something to recommend it.

items.label: Spring
items.name: The Essential Season
items.subtitle: Spring · Semana Santa and Feria de Abril
items.description: Semana Santa isn't a festival — it's the city stopping for a week to enact something it's been rehearsing for four centuries. Pasos weighing five tonnes, carried on shoulders, moving to bell taps. Pointed hoods, candles, total silence in the crowd — not enforced, just arrived. Two weeks later: Feria de Abril, an entire temporary city of casetas, dancing sevillanas until 6am. Outside the festivals, April and May are ideal: orange blossom, bearable heat, Alcázar not yet at capacity.

callout.label: Semana Santa — how to see it properly
callout.text: Processions follow fixed routes through the historic centre, all meeting at La Carrera Oficial. Best free viewing: side streets of Santa Cruz and Calle Sierpes. Arrive 45 minutes before the paso is due. Find a wall to lean against. Processions run Palm Sunday through Good Friday, sometimes until 3am. No ticket. No entrance fee. The city is the stage.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Survive or Avoid
items.subtitle: Summer · Plan Around the Heat
items.description: June: still manageable. July: 40°C regularly, Seville reorganises its entire day around this fact. Streets empty at 3pm. Streets full at 11pm. August is when Sevillanos who can afford to leave, leave. What remains runs on nocturnal logic: interesting if you understand it, brutal if you don't.

callout.label: Noches de Verano — Alcázar by night
callout.text: On selected summer evenings, the Alcázar opens after dark — Noches en los Jardines del Real Alcázar — live music, fountains lit, Mudejar arches cool. Ticketed, advance booking required. The version of the Alcázar most visitors never see.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: The Best-Kept Secret
items.subtitle: Autumn · When Seville Returns to Itself
items.description: City empties of tourists in late September. Alcázar bookable within days. Bars full of people with jobs here who know each other's names. October light arrives at a lower angle and catches the Cathedral stone at a colour summer never allows — between honey and rust. Tourist photographs of Seville are almost always taken in summer. October is why Sevillanos don't miss the tourists when they leave.

callout.label: Bienal de Flamenco (September, even years)
callout.text: In September of even-numbered years: Bienal de Flamenco — the world's largest flamenco festival, in the Teatro de la Maestranza and across the barrios. Headline shows sell out months ahead. Non-Bienal years still bring a full September programme across tablaos and peñas.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Quiet and Underrated
items.subtitle: Winter · Mild, Uncrowded, Entirely Local
items.description: December: chestnuts, orange blossom, Calle Sierpes lit up, Cathedral nativity scenes that take weeks to construct. Cabalgata de Reyes (5 Jan): most theatrical Three Kings parade in Andalusia. After the 6th: Alcázar same-day bookable, tapas bars returned to their owners, winter light so clear the city looks freshly washed. 15°C.

callout.label: Cabalgata de Reyes — 5 January
callout.text: 5 January evening: Three Kings parade through the historic centre, sweets thrown to children lining the streets. Spanish children receive presents this night, not Christmas Day — the anticipation weight is real. Free to watch. Go early for Calle Sierpes.

monthly_highlights.text: Semana Santa: the Holy Week processions lift the city into another dimension — grand, intense, unforgettable; hotels fill very early.
Feria de Abril: a week of flamenco dresses, horse carriages and rebujito at the fairground; the city at its most joyful.
Extreme heat: days above 40°C are normal; live mornings and nights, leave midday to the shade.
The ideal season: the heat breaks, the orange trees are still green, the squares are livable — the best months to visit.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: Sevillian food doesn't try to impress. Invented by people with very little: olive oil, chickpeas, offal, fish from 80km away. Arrived, over centuries, at something quietly extraordinary.

local_word.definition: The dry sherry Seville drinks — chilled, pale, bone-dry, faintly saline. Not British supermarket sherry. Manzanilla (from Sanlúcar, by the sea) is lighter and saltier still. In a Seville bar, a glass costs less than a bus ticket in most European capitals. Order it cold. The correct drink for everything in this city.

items.name: Espinacas con garbanzos — the Seville standard
items.description: Spinach and chickpeas in a sauce of fried bread, cumin, paprika, saffron, sherry vinegar. Moorish recipe, survived the Reconquista intact. Chickpeas absorb and thicken; spinach darkens and sweetens. Warm, with bread, in every traditional tapas bar. The version at El Rinconcillo (open 1670) made the same way since the bar opened. Never skip it.
items.tag: Every traditional bar · order with fino · Moorish roots

items.name: Jamón ibérico — the national obsession
items.description: Iberian pigs, acorn-fed in the dehesa forests of Extremadura. Two-year cure. The fat is oleic acid — same as olive oil. Melts at body temperature. In a good Seville bar it arrives with your drink, sliced thin on a small plate. Eat at room temperature. Cold is wrong.
items.tag: Ibérico de bellota · room temperature · with bread and olive oil

items.name: Pescaíto frito — fried fish, Andalusian style
items.description: Seville is 80km from the Atlantic. Fish arrives fresh. Andalusian technique: light flour coating, hot olive oil, a few seconds, out. Crisp outside, barely cooked within, no grease trace when done right. Boquerones, cazón en adobo, chocos. Standing in Triana, cold manzanilla, warm evening.
items.tag: Boquerones · cazón en adobo · cold beer · lemon

items.name: Salmorejo — Seville's answer to gazpacho
items.description: Gazpacho but with water removed and bread added. Blended until smooth, chilled until thick. Diced jamón and sliced egg on top. Deep brick-red. Should hold a spoon upright. Every restaurant in Seville makes it. A few are extraordinary.
items.tag: With egg and jamón · thicker than gazpacho · best cold

items.name: Fino sherry — the correct drink
items.description: Fino aged under flor yeast — stays pale, dry, saline instead of turning amber. Sea and cellar simultaneously. Order cold. Order another.
items.tag: Fino or manzanilla · always chilled · with everything

items.name: Torrijas and pestiños — convent sweets
items.description: During Semana Santa: convent tornos (revolving hatches) open. Place your order; the hatch turns; a hand you never see delivers it. Torrijas: wine-soaked bread, fried in olive oil, sugar and cinnamon. Heavier than French toast, better. Pestiños: honey-glazed dough with anise and sesame. Eaten warm outside the convent while processions pass.
items.tag: Convent tornos · Semana Santa tradition · anise and honey

callout.label: El Rinconcillo — the oldest tapas bar in Seville
callout.text: El Rinconcillo, Calle Gerona, 1670. System unchanged: order at the bar, bartender chalks the tally on the wood, settle at the end. One street from the tourist routes. Espinacas con garbanzos. Jamón. Croquetas. Prices are what they should be. Service isn't trying to charm you. Go Tuesday lunch. Take the stool nearest the barrel.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Gems
hidden_gems.intro: The Cathedral queue is one of the longest in Spain. Twenty metres away, through a passage, is a 16th-century arcaded square that almost no one enters. This is how Seville works.

items.rarity: A palace that rivals the Alcázar — and almost no one goes
items.name: Casa de Pilatos — Santa Cruz
items.description: The Medinaceli family measured the distance from their door to a local chapel and found it matched Pontius Pilate's house to Calvary. Named accordingly. Mudejar tilework, Gothic vaulting, Renaissance sculpture — shouldn't cohere, entirely does. Lawrence of Arabia filmed here. The Crown filmed here. The Alcázar gets 90% of the visitors. Ticketed. Free Mondays 15:00–19:00 — queue at the door.

items.rarity: Columbus's handwriting, on the wall, for free
items.name: Archivo General de Indias — Cathedral Square
items.description: Between the Cathedral and the Alcázar. Not a church, not a palace — a Renaissance archive with 80 million pages on Spain's colonisation of the Americas. Columbus's letters: behind glass, in his handwriting. Designed by Juan de Herrera (El Escorial's architect). The visitors in the Cathedral queue next door largely don't know it exists. Free Tuesday to Sunday.

items.rarity: The flamenco bar with no sign — and no tourists
items.name: La Carbonería — Santa Cruz
items.description: No sign. Wooden door on Calle Levíes. Looks like a private courtyard — because it is. Inside: former coal yard, mismatched chairs, exposed brick, free flamenco every evening. Audience: mostly local. Performers: not on the tourist-tablao circuit. Informal — guitarist finishes, someone calls for another song, they agree. No ticket. No reservation. Arrive, order, sit, pay attention.

items.rarity: A Moorish-inspired palace still owned by the poet's family
items.name: Palacio de las Dueñas — La Macarena
items.description: The Duchess of Alba lived here until 2014. 15th century, Mudéjar-Renaissance — orange-tree courtyards, jasmine-covered arches. Antonio Machado born here in 1875. Rooms hold the personal collections of the most decorated family in Spanish history: Goyas, Rubens, Roman sculpture. Ticketed. Free Mondays from 16:00 — book online same morning.

items.rarity: The city's oldest square — hidden inside the Cathedral's shadow
items.name: Plaza del Cabildo — Cathedral Square
items.description: South side of Cathedral square. Looks like a service entrance. Walk through — noise stops. 1572. A perfect semicircle of arches, designed for commerce, now a shortcut no one uses. Sunday mornings: a few stalls selling old coins and stamps. Otherwise: empty, quiet, surrounded by the highest tourist density in Andalusia. Seville in miniature. Free.

items.rarity: Seville from above — without the queue or the ticket
items.name: Metropol Parasol (Las Setas) — Plaza de la Encarnación
items.description: Six mushroom-shaped laminated timber parasols, 28 metres up, dividing Seville since 2011. Locals call it Las Setas. Most have made peace with it. Rooftop walkway: Giralda, Alcázar gardens, Guadalquivir, the white barrios south. Go an hour before sunset — the light on the Cathedral from up there. Rooftop ticketed. Ground floor market and Antiquarium Roman ruins: free.

callout.label: Triana — cross the bridge and stay
callout.text: Cross the Triana bridge. Walk one block: ceramics shops. Walk three blocks: Triana. Iron-and-glass market in a 19th-century castle gatehouse. Bars on Calle Betis facing the Cathedral — best view of the city, from the neighbourhood that always found the city slightly unnecessary. Flamenco peñas in the back streets — private clubs, serious practitioners, some admit visitors. Ask at the bar. Have dinner in Triana. Better food. Cheaper. No one trying to seat you.

items.label: Book the Alcázar before you arrive
items.sub: Ticketed, sells out weeks ahead. Monday from 16:00 free — but book free tickets online well in advance, limited capacity.

items.label: Eat espinacas con garbanzos at a traditional bar
items.sub: Spinach and chickpeas, Moorish recipe. El Rinconcillo (1670) or any traditional bar. With a glass of fino.

items.label: Visit Casa de Pilatos
items.sub: Ticketed. Monday 15:00–19:00 free, no booking — queue at the door. The Alcázar gets 90% of visitors.

items.label: Walk into Archivo General de Indias
items.sub: Between Cathedral and Alcázar. Columbus's letters on the wall. Free Tuesday to Sunday. Usually quieter than anything nearby.

items.label: Find La Carbonería on Calle Levíes
items.sub: Unmarked wooden door. Free flamenco every evening. No ticket, no reservation — arrive, order, watch.

items.label: Drink a glass of fino sherry at the bar
items.sub: Cold, dry, with whatever tapa arrives. Ask for fino or manzanilla. Price varies by bar.

items.label: Cross the Triana bridge and stay for dinner
items.sub: Mercado de Triana, Calle Betis, Cathedral views. Better food, cheaper than Santa Cruz. Free to walk.

items.label: Find Plaza del Cabildo
items.sub: Narrow passage near Cathedral entrance. Semicircular arcaded square. Free. Crowd is fifteen seconds away and doesn't know it's here.

items.label: Visit Palacio de las Dueñas
items.sub: Ticketed. Monday from 16:00 free — book online same morning. Almost unknown to non-Spanish visitors.

items.label: Walk the Guadalquivir path an hour before sunset
items.sub: Torre del Oro south to Triana bridge. SEVIci bike or on foot. Free. The stone turns a colour with no name in English.

items.label: Go to El Rinconcillo on a weekday
items.sub: Calle Gerona. Open since 1670. Tab chalked on the bar. Stool nearest the barrel. Price varies.

items.label: Watch sunset from Metropol Parasol (Las Setas)
items.sub: Rooftop ticketed. Ground floor and Roman ruins free. Go an hour before sunset.

items.label: Walk through the Alcázar
items.sub: Ticketed, advance booking required. Mudejar tilework, horseshoe arches, reflecting pools. The most extraordinary palace in Spain outside Granada.

items.label: Enter the Cathedral
items.sub: The largest Gothic building in the world. Ticketed, advance booking recommended. Columbus's tomb is inside.

items.label: Drink a cheap beer on the Alameda de Hércules
items.sub: Europe's oldest public promenade (1574). Now lined with bars. Sit, watch, prices are half of the centre.

items.label: Visit the Torre del Oro
items.sub: 13th-century Golden Tower on the riverfront. Ticketed. Free all day Monday, no reservation needed.

traps.title: Skip the Traps
traps.intro: Seville is a welcoming city, but the classic games run in its tourist-heavy corners. Know these four and live Andalusia like a local.

items.name: Dinner-package 'flamenco shows'
items.description: At the shows staged for bus tourists, flamenco becomes background music: frozen paella, a miked-up act, no soul.
items.instead: Watch flamenco where it was born: a small tablao or a place like La Carbonería, drink in hand, two metres from the stage.

items.name: Boarding a carriage without agreeing the price
items.description: The horse carriages are a lovely classic, but board without talking money and the tour shortens while the bill grows.
items.instead: Ask for the official tariff and settle it before boarding; or walk the same route — Santa Cruz exists to be walked.

items.name: 'Menú turístico' right by the Cathedral and Alcázar
items.description: The photo menus at the monument exits mean microwave paella and a swollen bill; nothing to do with Seville's tapas soul.
items.instead: Walk two streets: lean on a bar in Alfalfa, El Arenal, or across the river in Triana, and order tapas.

items.name: Sightseeing at summer midday
items.description: In July and August the thermometer passes 40°C between 2 and 6 pm; queueing for monuments then melts your holiday.
items.instead: Live like the city: sightsee early, take a long lunch and siesta somewhere cool, return to the streets at night — Seville blooms after dark.

callout.label: The golden rule
callout.text: The mark of a good bar in Seville is a standing crowd and napkins on the floor: if the counter is packed and the floor is littered, the kitchen is good — stay.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: Palaces, orange courtyards and midnight flamenco

steps.title: Real Alcázar — first slot
steps.description: Book weeks ahead and take the first entry: the gardens in the morning cool, before the crowds, are paradise itself.

steps.title: Cathedral + Giralda
steps.description: The world's largest Gothic cathedral, then climb the ramped tower: Seville at your feet.

steps.title: Long lunch + siesta
steps.description: Match the city's rhythm: salmorejo, espinacas, a glass of fino. Then no hurry — the hottest hours pass in the shade.

steps.title: Plaza de España + María Luisa Park
steps.description: Ceramic bridges and the canal in evening light; the city's most generous photo stage.

steps.title: Tapas crawl in Triana
steps.description: Cross the bridge, go bar to bar around Calle Betis and the market: pescaíto frito + cold beer.

steps.title: Flamenco at night
steps.description: A small tablao or La Carbonería: the thing they call duende only comes out at this hour.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Live the city as a guest, not a tourist

steps.title: The classics
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: Alcázar, Cathedral, Plaza de España, Triana.

steps.title: Palaces and Macarena
steps.description: Casa de Pilatos and Palacio de las Dueñas in the morning, the Macarena quarter and basilica in the afternoon, a sunset walk on top of Las Setas.

steps.title: The river and goodbye
steps.description: Torre del Oro and the riverside in the morning, Triana market and ceramic workshops at noon, an Arab bath in the afternoon, one last tapas crawl in Alfalfa at night.

phrases.title: The 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Spanish is sung here rather than spoken; these five open Andalusian doors.

items.meaning: The short all-day greeting — entering any shop or bar
Thank you — in the Andalusian accent: grasya
Please — add it to the end of your order
Cheers! — fino glasses rise to this
No worries / never mind — the Andalusian philosophy of life in one phrase
